headline: College majors now obsolete before graduation, students panic rationally
subheadline: The education industrial complex discovers it cannot sell four-year insurance policies against six-month technology cycles.
source_headline: There's no point: AI forces college students to rethink their major
body_html:
Somewhere between freshman orientation and sophomore organic chemistry, American college students have arrived at a conclusion that should have been obvious in 2016: spending $80,000 to $200,000 on a four-year degree as insurance against technological disruption is perhaps the worst hedge in financial history. According to Axios reporting, students and their parents are now actively searching for "future-proof" majors in an AI-powered world. This is not a thought experiment. This is the actual behavior of rational actors realizing that the foundational promise of higher education—that your diploma is a durable asset—has evaporated faster than a ChatGPT API response.

The irony is exquisite. For decades, the college-industrial complex sold itself on precisely one value proposition: prepare your children for a world we cannot predict by teaching them skills we cannot define. Parents mortgaged homes. Students took six-figure loans. Administrators built luxury dorms and hired vice provosts of strategic innovation. The entire edifice was built on the assumption that a degree in Business Administration, Communications, or (God help us) Information Technology would retain value for at least four years—long enough to recoup the investment. AI has made that assumption laughable. The entry-level job market is now moving faster than accreditation committees can blink, and no college dean has yet announced a major in "Skills That Might Be Relevant by the Time You Graduate," because it would be impossible to staff.

What's particularly savage about this moment is that it reveals the deeper con: colleges were never actually preparing students for the future. They were selling credentials for the present, dressed up in futurist rhetoric. "We teach you how to think," they promised, which is the higher-education equivalent of a car salesman saying "the engine isn't important—it's about your journey." Students have now called this bluff. If AI is going to obsolete your skills in 18 months regardless, why waste four years and $150,000 on a major? Why not just learn whatever's hot right now, assume it's dead in 36 months, and plan accordingly? The calculus has inverted.

The colleges' response, per Axios, is "rethinking how to prepare students for the transition." Translation: we have no idea what we're doing and we're terrified of enrollment cliffs. Notice they're not offering refunds or apologizing for 40 years of overpromising. They're tinkering with curriculum while the fundamental business model—sell expensive, slow-moving credentials in a fast-moving economy—collapses beneath them. A student switching majors because AI will make their chosen field unrecognizable is not experiencing an education crisis. They're experiencing rational skepticism toward an institution that has bet everything on being able to predict the future and failed catastrophically.

Here's what makes this particularly beautiful from a VC perspective: this crisis is the natural endpoint of the venture capital belief that technology solves everything, including itself. Silicon Valley spent the last 15 years insisting that AI would disrupt every industry and eliminate entire job categories. Students and parents listened. Now they're acting on that belief by refusing to specialize in anything—because why should they, if specialization is dead? The education sector is discovering what happens when you sell everyone on exponential change and then those people take it seriously enough to stop buying your product.

The real kicker: there is no future-proof major in an AI-powered world. There is only the honest acknowledgment that a $150,000 credential program cannot outrun a technology that improves monthly. Colleges could admit this and reinvent themselves as something other than degree factories. Or they can keep pretending a degree in "AI-Ready Problem Solving" is different from a degree in anything else, watch enrollment plummet, and discover that the only thing truly future-proof in American higher education is tuition price increases.
glossary_definition: A college degree that will be obsolete by the time you finish paying for it.
